analysis.one_liner: Requires paper ballots, hand-count audits of federal elections, and grants to states for voting system security.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in two years and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal election law to require every voting machine used in federal elections to produce a paper ballot the voter can check before it is counted. It would require states to hand-count paper ballots in randomly selected precincts after each federal election, with the federal government paying the audit costs, and would bar states from buying paperless electronic voting machines. It also authorizes grants to help states update equipment, keep offline backups of voter rolls, and secure vote reporting, and directs the Department of Homeland Security to notify Congress and state election officials of breaches or breach investigations.
analysis.who_benefits: All voters in federal elections get a voter-verifiable paper ballot that is preserved as the official record and hand-counted in audits, making results harder to alter by machine error or hacking. State election offices receive federal money to cover audit costs and competitive grants for equipment upgrades and security improvements. Ordinary people get public observation of audits and published results before certification.

how_it_helps.text: Voting systems in federal elections must use individual, durable, voter-verified paper ballots that the voter can inspect before casting, and the paper ballot becomes the official record used in any recount or audit [S2][S3].

Beginning in November 2022, states must audit results of competitive federal races through random hand counts of paper ballots, with the Election Assistance Commission paying the states' audit costs [S2][S3].
States may no longer purchase electronic voting systems without a voter-verified paper record for use in federal elections [S2][S3].

The Election Assistance Commission awards competitive grants to states for security steps such as machines under 10 years old, offline backups of voter registration lists, secure vote-tally reporting, and chain-of-custody procedures [S3].

If Homeland Security determines or investigates a breach of a state's voting system or voter database, it must report to Congress and the state election office, and must collaborate with states on request to prevent and respond to threats [S2][S3].
Audits must be conducted without advance notice to selected precincts, allow public observation, be published, and no state may certify results before the audit is complete [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the audit payments (a $45 million annual authorization) and the state security grants; election officials bear new operational work, and jurisdictions using paperless machines must buy or replace equipment within a year of enactment. Election technology vendors selling paperless machines lose a market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and voting machine vendors

drawbacks.text: The mandate is costly and fast: every jurisdiction must use voter-verifiable paper ballots within one year of enactment, and small or rural election offices may struggle to buy and staff equipment on that timeline [S3].
The audit subtitle authorizes $45 million per year for state payments, an ongoing federal appropriation, and hand-counted audits add labor and expense for election administrators [S3].

Requiring audits and certification delays gives losing campaigns more time to contest results, and the paper-record rules add procedures (such as establishing the paper ballot as the true record in discrepancies) that critics could argue complicate close elections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real vulnerability — tampering or errors in paperless machines that leave no way to check the count — and pays states rather than simply mandating costs on them, which blunts the burden. The one-year deadline for universal paper ballots is aggressive and the audit funding depends on future appropriations, so the main honest objections are cost and feasibility, not that the protections are weak. On balance the safeguards outweigh the costs, though the timeline was ambitious.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration and Science committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee a month later, and neither committee ever acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the Safeguarding Election Infrastructure Act of 2019 on January 9, 2019 [S1][S5].

It was referred to the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, and on February 12, 2019 was referred to the Subcommittee on Research and Technology [S1][S5].
No further action was recorded, and the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Election offices and vendors relying on existing equipment avoided the new paper-ballot and audit requirements, and the federal government avoided the audit and grant spending. Voters got none of the paper-ballot and audit protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing election equipment and its vendors

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 9, 2019 to require paper ballots, mandatory hand-count audits, and state security grants.

against.name: Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 9, 2019 and never held a markup or advanced the bill.

against.name: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee / Subcommittee on Research and Technology
against.role: House committee and subcommittee of referral
against.what_they_did: Received a portion of the referral; the subcommittee received it on February 12, 2019 and no action followed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so partisan positions were never recorded [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill bans purchases of paperless electronic voting machines for federal elections and requires voter-verifiable paper ballots within a year, forcing vendors to sell different systems. That cost is the flip side of voters getting an auditable paper record.

The bill creates federal grant-funded work — equipment updates, secure databases, offline backups — and requires audits that states may conduct with existing personnel. New public money flows toward election security services.
